recorded: Late 1953 or January 1954, Salle Adyar, Paris
intro: Couperin wrote Le Tic-Toc-Choc, ou Les Maillotins for two hands playing in the same register of the harpsichord on separate manuals, with a refrain and three episodes. Marcelle Meyer plays it on the piano.

sections.label: A · Refrain in semiquavers
sections.mNote: Semiquavers above a slower left-hand pattern.

sections.label: A′ · Refrain with added ending
sections.mNote: A supplément extends the last return of the refrain.

cues.title: Opening marking and refrain
cues.text: A stream of semiquavers runs above a slower left-hand pattern. Couperin marks the piece Légèrement et marqué, lightly and with clear accents. The F major refrain returns between three episodes.
cues.evidence: Couperin, Troisième Livre (1722), XVIIIe Ordre; Pierre Gouin edition, pp. 1–3: opening marking, rondeau and three couplets. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ec/IMSLP128601-WIMA.a398-Couperin_18eOrdre_Le_TicTocChoc.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Preface on two keyboards, 1722
cues.text: In the preface to his 1722 book, Couperin assigned his pièces croisées to two harpsichord keyboards, so that both hands could occupy the same notes without colliding. For an instrument with only one keyboard, he allowed one part to be moved an octave away.
cues.evidence: Couperin’s preface to the Troisième Livre, quoted with its performance instructions and original notation by harpsichord maker Carey Beebe. https://www.hpschd.nu/tech/rsc/tic.html

cues.title: Final refrain and supplément
cues.text: The final refrain has a short supplément, an extra ending. The semiquavers continue into it, and then both hands hold an F major chord.
cues.evidence: Gouin edition, p. 3, from “Rondeau sans Renvoi avec le Supplément” to the final F-major chord. Angela Hewitt also describes the added coda in her Hyperion notes. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67440
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Musician who played for Louis XIV on Sundays, known at the harpsichord for held notes, trills and well-placed silences.
facts: Son of Charles Couperin; nephew of Louis; organist at Saint-Gervais from 1685
Royal chapel organist from 1693; chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books, 1713–30: 27 ordres; L’Art de toucher le clavecin, 1716–17
Two organ masses; Leçons de Ténèbres; chamber concerts and viol suites
composer.background:
On Sundays in 1714 and 1715, François Couperin played chamber music for the ageing Louis XIV. The violinist François Duval joined him, with wind players and a viol; Couperin played the harpsichord. When he published the Concerts royaux in 1722, he recalled that the king had summoned him “almost every Sunday of the year”. The dances in the collection, among them an allemande, a grave sarabande and a little chaconne, had been played in the king’s rooms. Louis XIV had once danced in his own court ballets.

Couperin was born in Paris in 1668, into a family already established at the organ of Saint-Gervais. His uncle Louis had held the post before his father Charles, and had died before François was born. When Charles died in 1679, the church kept the succession open for the boy, and Michel-Richard de Lalande covered the duties until he was ready. François studied with Jacques Thomelin and took over in 1685. At twenty-five he won one of the four organists’ places at the royal chapel. He kept his Paris work, travelled to court for his quarter of service and taught the royal children.
